records.why: The ugali analogy was misleading: when ugali is cooked, mass is conserved (the lost mass is just steam), so it teaches the opposite of mass defect and reinforces a misconception. A numbers example shows how much energy a tiny mass gives. Checked: c² = (3 × 10⁸)² = 9 × 10¹⁶; 0.001 × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 9 × 10¹³ J; 9 × 10¹³ J ÷ 100 W = 9 × 10¹¹ s ≈ 28 500 years (one year ≈ 3.16 × 10⁷ s).
records.old: PART B — Mass Defect and E = mc² (Conceptual, 8 minutes): The teacher uses a 'Ugali analogy' to explain mass defect conceptually: 'Imagine you have 1 kg of ugali flour and 0.5 kg of water. You combine them and cook. The ugali you get out weighs slightly LESS than the combined ingredients — where did that mass go? It was released as heat and steam. In nuclear reactions, the products weigh SLIGHTLY less than the reactants — and that tiny lost mass becomes an ENORMOUS amount of energy, because energy = mass × the speed of light SQUARED. The speed of light is 300,000,000 metres per second — squared. Even a tiny mass becomes colossal energy.' Learners annotate this analogy in their notebooks and write E = mc² with a verbal definition.
records.new: PART B — Mass Defect and E = mc² (Conceptual, 6 minutes): The teacher explains mass defect with a worked example instead of a cooking comparison: 'In a chemical reaction, such as cooking ugali, the total mass at the end is the same as at the start (the steam that escapes still has mass). In a nuclear reaction the products really do weigh slightly LESS than the starting nucleus, and that missing mass becomes energy: E = mc². The speed of light is 300 000 000 m/s, so c² is 9 × 10¹⁶. If only 1 gram (0.001 kg) of mass became energy, E = 0.001 × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 9 × 10¹³ joules, enough to keep a 100 W bulb lit for about 28 000 years.' Learners write E = mc² with a verbal definition and copy the worked example into their notebooks. (Limit of the picture: the missing mass is not material that escapes; it is mass that has become energy.)
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 3, ch. 10 (mass-energy equivalence, mass defect); law of conservation of mass in chemical reactions

records.why: This answers the audit item. The old exemplar changed direction midway and never said what the plot shows about the belt. The new answer keeps the correct N/Z numbers and ends with the chain reaching stable lead-206. Checked: 238 - 206 = 32 = 8 alpha x 4; Z 92 - (8 x 2) + 6 = 82, so 6 beta-minus decays; N = 206 - 82 = 124; N/Z values 146/92 = 1.587, 144/90 = 1.600, 143/91 = 1.571.
records.old: (d) On the N vs Z graph, uranium-238 lies outside the belt of stability. Alpha decay reduces both N and Z by 2, so the nucleus moves diagonally down and to the left on the plot. Beta-minus decay lowers N by 1 and raises Z by 1, so the nucleus moves one step diagonally down and to the right. Each decay gives a daughter nucleus plotted in a new position, so the nucleus changes its composition step by step along the chain. Checking the neutron-to-proton ratio shows that not every single step moves it in the same direction: for uranium-238, N/Z = 146/92 ≈ 1.59, and for thorium-234, N/Z = 144/90 = 1.60, so the first alpha step does not clearly move the nucleus toward the belt in ratio terms. The beta step to protactinium-234 gives N/Z = 143/91 ≈ 1.57, so the ratio falls. The daughters may still be unstable and decay again, and the chain as a whole continues until a stable nucleus is reached. Gamma emission does not move the nucleus on the plot; it carries away excess energy during these changes.
records.new: (d) On the N vs Z graph, uranium-238 (Z = 92, N = 146) lies beyond the end of the belt of stability: no nuclide with Z above 83 is stable. Alpha decay reduces both N and Z by 2, so the nucleus moves diagonally down and to the left on the plot. Beta-minus decay lowers N by 1 and raises Z by 1, so the nucleus moves one step diagonally down and to the right. Individual steps do not all lower the neutron-to-proton ratio: uranium-238 has N/Z = 146/92 ≈ 1.59, thorium-234 has 144/90 = 1.60 and protactinium-234 has 143/91 ≈ 1.57. What matters is the whole chain: the nucleus changes composition step by step (8 alpha and 6 beta-minus decays in all) until it reaches stable lead-206 (Z = 82, N = 124), which lies inside the belt of stability. This shows that decay is the nucleus's route to a stable arrangement, and that the daughters of uranium-238 are themselves unstable until the chain ends. Gamma emission does not move the nucleus on the plot; it carries away excess energy during these changes.
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 3, ch. 10 (nuclear stability, uranium-238 decay series ending at lead-206); no stable nuclide exists above bismuth-209 (Z = 83)

records.old:
• Meaning of radioactivity and the structure of the nucleus (protons, neutrons, nucleon number, proton number)
• Isotopes: definition, examples (e.g. Carbon-12 and Carbon-14), and the concept of nuclear stability
• Neutron-to-proton (N/Z) ratio and construction of the belt (valley) of stability
• Types of nuclear radiation: alpha (α), beta (β), and gamma (γ) — properties, charge, mass, and penetrating power
• Detection of radiation: Geiger-Müller counter, cloud chamber, and photographic film — working principles and applications
• Radioactive decay and half-life: decay curves, calculations, and real-world significance
• Nuclear equations: writing and balancing equations for α-decay, β-decay, and γ-emission
• Nuclear fission and nuclear fusion: energy release, comparison, and global/Kenyan energy relevance
• Applications of radioactivity: medicine (cancer treatment, PET scans), agriculture (food irradiation, soil tracing), industry, and carbon dating
• Radiation safety: effects of radiation on living tissue, protection measures, and responsible handling of radioactive materials

records.why: KICD names two core competencies for this sub-strand (Imagination and Creativity; Self-efficacy). They were missing; the existing five are kept below as additional competencies, and the KICD two are tied to real activities.
records.value:
• Imagination and Creativity: the learner develops the skill of making connections by finding hidden patterns between different ideas while making charts that illustrate properties of radioactive radiations. (In this unit: Lesson 1 belt of stability plot, Lesson 2 Evidence Table and Radiation Properties Legend.)
• Self-efficacy: the learner develops self-awareness and acquires planning skill while searching and discussing in groups safety precautions when handling radioactive substances. (In this unit: Lesson 7 radiation safety design task.)
Also developed in this unit (not in the KICD list for this sub-strand):
• Communication and Collaboration: Learners work in groups to compare α, β, and γ radiation properties, construct the belt of stability, and present findings on radiation applications — embracing teamwork and contributing to shared group decisions.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: Learners analyse neutron-to-proton ratios to predict nuclear stability, interpret decay curves to calculate half-life, and balance nuclear equations — developing logical reasoning and quantitative problem-solving skills.
• Learning to Learn: Learners use PhET simulations, Khan Academy resources, and YouTube videos to independently investigate radioactive decay and half-life, practising self-directed inquiry and knowledge construction.
• Digital Literacy: Learners interact with digital tools (PhET Nuclear Fission simulation, online decay curve plotters) to visualise abstract nuclear processes, building competency in using technology for scientific investigation.
• Citizenship: Learners evaluate radiation safety protocols and the ethical use of nuclear technology in Kenyan hospitals and research institutions, developing informed and responsible civic perspectives on science and society.

records.why: KICD PCIs for this sub-strand are Citizenship education and Socio-Economic and Environmental issues; the second was missing and the first was paraphrased. Restored and tied to lessons; the other PCIs are kept as additional.
records.value:
• Citizenship education: the learner practises peace and conflict resolution mechanisms as ways of promoting peace while searching from print and non-print media, on applications of radioactivity. (In this unit: Lesson 6 structured academic controversy; Lesson 7 applications carousel.)
• Socio-Economic and Environmental issues: the learner demonstrates environmental conservation awareness as they search, discuss in groups and present findings on safety precautions when handling and disposing of radioactive substances. (In this unit: Lesson 7 safety plan, including waste disposal.)
Also developed in this unit (not in the KICD list for this sub-strand):
• Health Education: Learners discuss the biological effects of ionising radiation on human tissue and the importance of radiation safety in medical facilities such as Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) and Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, promoting health-conscious decision-making.
• Environmental Education: Learners examine how radioactive contamination can affect ecosystems (e.g., water sources like Lake Victoria and the Tana River) and discuss responsible waste disposal of radioactive materials.
• Life Skills — Critical Thinking and Decision Making: Learners evaluate competing claims about nuclear energy as a solution to Kenya's energy challenges versus its safety and environmental risks, building informed decision-making skills.
• Career Guidance: Learners identify and explore career pathways in nuclear medicine, radiography, radiation protection, and nuclear engineering — including opportunities at the Kenya Nuclear Electricity Board (KNEB) and local universities offering relevant programmes.
• Disaster Risk Reduction: Learners assess the risks of radiation exposure in emergency scenarios and develop awareness of safety protocols, connecting to national disaster preparedness frameworks.

records.why: CBE levels are Exceeds, Meets, Approaches and Below Expectations. The rubric headings are fixed by the template, so the level name is now written at the start of each descriptor (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches) to match CBE language.

value.criterion: Explaining why the nucleus is unstable
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Accurately explains nucleons, isotopes and the belt of stability, and clearly links the neutron-to-proton ratio of uranium-238 to spontaneous decay as a nuclear, not chemical, process.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains isotopes and instability correctly but the link to the belt of stability or to the nuclear nature of decay is incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Describes radioactivity without explaining nuclear instability or confuses isotopes with other ideas.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly compares alpha, beta and gamma, writes balanced equations with conserved A and Z, and explains decay arrows on the N vs Z plot.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Compares radiation types correctly and writes mostly correct equations with minor errors in balancing or in explaining movement on the plot.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Lists some properties but equations are unbalanced or missing, and no link to stability is made.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Explains the GM tube process, background correction and half-life using the dice evidence, and correctly calculates the fraction remaining.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains most of detection and half-life correctly; the calculation or the use of simulation evidence has small gaps.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives vague statements about detection or half-life; calculation is missing or incorrect.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Links mass defect and E = mc² to the rock's energy, distinguishes fission from fusion, and gives Kenyan applications and ALARA measures with correct reasoning.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives correct applications and safety measures, with only partial explanation of mass defect or of fission versus fusion.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Names applications or safety ideas without explanation, or with errors.

value.criterion: Communication and connection to the phenomenon
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Writes clearly in logical order, uses scientific vocabulary precisely, and consistently ties each idea back to the pitchblende rock and Kenyan contexts.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Writing is mostly clear and uses key terms; links to the phenomenon are present but not consistent.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Writing is hard to follow, with little scientific vocabulary or connection to the rock.

records.why: The partner contract only allows three rubric levels (excellent, proficient, developing), so the fourth CBE level, Below Expectations, cannot be represented in the data or printed rubric. Suggested workaround: teachers treat any answer below the Approaches descriptor as Below Expectations. A change to the contract or template would be needed to print it.

Strand and sub-strand numbering does not match KICD. This module says "Strand 3.0: Electricity and Magnetism, Sub-Strand 3.1", but in the KICD Grade 10 Physics design this topic is Sub-Strand 2.2 Radioactivity and Stability of Isotopes under Strand 2.0 Waves and Optics (Strand 3.0 starts with 3.1 Electrostatics). Not renamed because the numbering is used in file names and every lesson; teachers to decide whether to renumber. Also Lesson 4 writes the sub-strand as "3.1 Radioactivity..." without the words "Sub-Strand".

KICD content or activities not taught or assessed: (1) detection by leaf electroscope, and photographic film/plate taught as a detection method (the film is only the phenomenon); (2) the half-life demonstration by timing water running from a burette (the dice model replaces it); (3) using real half-life data from print or non-print media; (4) a uranium natural decay series chart (only three steps of the chain are shown); (5) the Chernobyl case study is only an evidence card in Lesson 6. Adding them would lengthen already full lessons, so the choice is left to teachers (e.g. leaf electroscope as an optional demonstration in Lesson 3, burette demonstration as homework in Lesson 4).

Please check the simulations before teaching. Lesson 6: in the PhET Nuclear Fission simulation, control rods and the reactor are on the Nuclear Reactor tab, not on the Chain Reaction tab where Step 3 places them, and I could not confirm that the simulation shows steam and a turbine (Step 4); a short video may need to supply that. Lesson 5, Evidence Activity 3: I know of no PhET simulation where learners type in a parent nucleus and read off the daughter; the "ARES offline module" must exist or the activity should become a worksheet table of three decays.
